subject: Neurology
stem: A 73-year-old woman is admitted after a pontine infarct. She is alert, follows commands, and can lift all four limbs. Her speech remains mildly slurred, but she denies trouble swallowing. A family member brings soup while the nurse prepares oral aspirin. No swallowing assessment has been documented. Oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. What should occur before she receives anything by mouth?

options.text: Allow small sips because she denies dysphagia
options.explanation: Patients may have impaired awareness or silent aspiration; a symptom report alone cannot establish safe swallowing after a brainstem infarct.

options.text: Give prophylactic antibiotics and proceed with lunch
options.explanation: Antibiotics do not restore airway protection or prevent aspiration events, and routine prophylaxis is not a substitute for swallowing assessment.

options.text: Start thickened liquids without any assessment
options.explanation: Texture changes should follow individualized evaluation; empirically thickening all liquids can still permit aspiration and may reduce hydration or intake.

options.text: Perform a validated swallowing screen by trained staff
options.explanation: Alertness and limb strength do not exclude pharyngeal dysfunction; screening should precede food, fluids, and oral medications after acute stroke.

explanation: Brainstem stroke can disrupt coordinated swallowing despite preserved consciousness and relatively good limb strength. A validated screen performed by trained personnel identifies patients who need a formal dysphagia assessment before oral intake. Food, drinks, and oral drugs all pose aspiration risk. Failure of a screen should trigger an alternative medication and hydration plan plus specialist evaluation, rather than prolonged unsupported fasting. Neither normal oxygen saturation nor absence of reported choking proves that aspiration is absent; aspiration can be silent.
objective: Screen swallowing before oral intake after acute stroke even when alertness and limb strength appear reassuring.
keyPoints: Swallowing safety requires assessment separate from the limb examination.
A failed screen requires a hydration and nutrition plan.

subject: Neurology
stem: Five days after an ischemic stroke, a 59-year-old man remains unable to swallow safely on specialist assessment. He is awake, participates in therapy, and has a functioning gastrointestinal tract. The rehabilitation team expects swallowing to improve during the next two weeks. He has received insufficient calories despite intravenous maintenance fluids. There is no facial trauma or gastrointestinal obstruction. Which feeding strategy is most appropriate now?

options.text: Place a permanent gastrostomy immediately in every stroke patient
options.explanation: Gastrostomy may suit prolonged dysphagia, but an invasive long-term route is premature when improvement is expected within a short interval.

options.text: Begin total parenteral nutrition despite available enteral access
options.explanation: Parenteral nutrition introduces catheter and metabolic risks and is generally unnecessary when the gastrointestinal tract can provide adequate enteral nutrition.

options.text: Provide temporary nasogastric enteral feeding with reassessment
options.explanation: A functioning gut and likely short duration of unsafe swallowing favor temporary enteral access while recovery and nutritional adequacy are reassessed.

options.text: Continue maintenance saline alone until swallowing returns
options.explanation: Maintenance fluids do not provide sufficient protein or energy; waiting without nutrition exposes this recovering patient to avoidable nutritional deterioration.

explanation: Unsafe swallowing does not require withholding nutrition when the gastrointestinal tract works. Temporary nasogastric feeding supports energy, protein, fluids, and appropriate medications during early recovery, with ongoing swallowing therapy and reassessment. Gastrostomy can be considered when prolonged inability to eat is anticipated, taking prognosis and patient preferences into account. Feeding tubes do not eliminate aspiration of oral secretions or reflux, so positioning, oral care, and monitoring remain important. The decision tests the expected duration and usable route, rather than assuming intravenous fluids constitute nutritional support.
objective: Choose temporary enteral access for early poststroke dysphagia when the gut functions and recovery is expected soon.
keyPoints: Intravenous maintenance fluids are not complete nutrition.
Reassess swallowing and feeding goals over time.

subject: Neurology
stem: A 31-year-old woman presents nine days after delivery with a steadily worsening headache and a new focal seizure involving her right hand. Blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg; she has no fever or proteinuria. Examination reveals mild right arm weakness and optic disc swelling. CT shows a small left frontal hemorrhagic lesion extending across an arterial boundary. Which study best evaluates the leading diagnosis?

options.text: Lumbar puncture before further imaging
options.explanation: Papilledema, focal deficit, and an intracranial hemorrhagic lesion require imaging-based evaluation before considering lumbar puncture for alternative diagnoses.

options.text: MR venography of the cerebral venous system
options.explanation: Progressive postpartum headache, papilledema, focal seizure, and a hemorrhagic lesion outside a single arterial territory suggest cerebral venous thrombosis.

options.text: Routine outpatient electroencephalography as the sole investigation
options.explanation: EEG may characterize seizures but does not evaluate the underlying venous obstruction responsible for raised pressure and this hemorrhagic infarct pattern.

options.text: Carotid ultrasonography without intracranial venous imaging
options.explanation: Carotid disease causes arterial ischemic patterns and does not adequately investigate dural sinus thrombosis or explain raised intracranial pressure here.

explanation: Pregnancy-associated hypercoagulability can persist postpartum and predispose to cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Venous outflow obstruction raises intracranial pressure and can cause hemorrhagic infarction that does not respect arterial territories. MR venography, or an appropriate CT venographic protocol when indicated, directly evaluates the venous system. Normal blood pressure and absent proteinuria make a hypertensive pregnancy-related syndrome less persuasive, although postpartum headache still requires a broad assessment. The seizure is a consequence to treat, not an adequate explanation for the evolving headache and imaging abnormality.
objective: Investigate suspected postpartum cerebral venous thrombosis with dedicated venous imaging when symptoms and hemorrhage distribution are nonarterial.
keyPoints: Venous infarcts can be hemorrhagic.
Routine arterial studies do not replace venography.

subject: Neurology
stem: A 44-year-old man with epilepsy has continuous generalized convulsions for eight minutes. Oxygen, suction, monitoring, and intravenous access are established. Bedside glucose is 112 mg/dL. An adequate weight-based dose of intravenous lorazepam is given and repeated according to protocol, but convulsions continue. Blood pressure is 136/84 mm Hg. Which action is most appropriate while the team prepares for possible airway escalation?

options.text: Load an intravenous second-line antiseizure drug such as levetiracetam
options.explanation: Persistent convulsive status after adequate benzodiazepine treatment requires rapid escalation to a longer-acting intravenous antiseizure agent with continued airway monitoring.

options.text: Wait thirty minutes for a routine EEG before further medication
options.explanation: Visible ongoing generalized convulsions establish the emergency; delaying treatment for diagnostic recording prolongs seizures and increases physiological and neuronal injury risk.

options.text: Give oral maintenance tablets and observe for absorption
options.explanation: Oral absorption is too slow and unsafe during convulsions, and a maintenance dose does not provide the rapid loading needed.

options.text: Give intravenous dextrose as the only next seizure treatment
options.explanation: Dextrose treats hypoglycemic seizures, but the measured glucose is normal; it does not replace second-line antiseizure loading for ongoing benzodiazepine-resistant convulsions.

explanation: Convulsive status epilepticus is treated as a time-sensitive emergency. Benzodiazepines are initial therapy, but persistent seizures after adequate dosing require prompt intravenous second-line loading rather than repeated delays. Levetiracetam is one accepted option; other choices depend on contraindications and protocol. Airway support, temperature and metabolic assessment, trigger investigation, and readiness for refractory-status treatment proceed concurrently. EEG is important when clinical convulsions stop without recovery or when refractory status is suspected, but it should not delay treatment of unmistakable ongoing generalized convulsions.
objective: Escalate persistent convulsive status promptly after adequate initial benzodiazepine therapy.
keyPoints: Treat the seizure while investigating its trigger.
Use a rapid intravenous loading strategy when initial therapy fails.

subject: Neurology
stem: A 70-year-old man is treated for a prolonged focal-to-bilateral convulsion. Visible shaking stops after medication, but forty minutes later he still does not follow commands. Oxygenation, blood pressure, glucose, sodium, and temperature are normal. CT shows no acute hemorrhage. The nurse notices repeated brief left eyelid twitching and gaze deviation. Which investigation should be obtained urgently to explain his persistent impaired responsiveness?

options.text: Repeat structural CT as the sole evaluation before considering EEG
options.explanation: Structural imaging may be repeated if new findings warrant it, but a recent unrevealing CT cannot identify ongoing electrical seizures causing the recurring stereotyped signs.

options.text: Perform lumbar puncture before considering electrical seizure monitoring
options.explanation: CSF studies may be appropriate for a suspected infectious trigger, but no infectious features are provided and they do not identify ongoing electrical status.

options.text: Observe as an uncomplicated postictal state without further investigation
options.explanation: Postictal recovery varies, but assuming that explanation without reassessment risks missing nonconvulsive status, especially with persistent stereotyped twitching and gaze deviation.

options.text: Continuous or urgent electroencephalographic monitoring
options.explanation: Persistent impaired consciousness with recurring subtle motor signs can represent ongoing electrical seizures despite cessation of generalized visible convulsions.

explanation: Stopping visible convulsions does not guarantee that cerebral seizure activity has ended. Nonconvulsive status can produce persistent coma, confusion, or small repetitive movements and is confirmed by EEG interpreted in the clinical context. Medication sedation and a postictal state remain alternatives, but normal bedside metabolic results do not distinguish them from ongoing electrical seizures. Urgent monitoring can identify a treatable cause and guide therapy. The recurrent stereotyped focal signs make passive observation particularly unsafe, even though the initial convulsion has apparently resolved.
objective: Use urgent EEG to evaluate suspected nonconvulsive status after apparent termination of convulsive seizures.
keyPoints: Clinical motor cessation does not prove electrical seizure cessation.
Reassess delayed recovery rather than labeling it automatically postictal.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: A 36-year-old woman taking valproate for generalized epilepsy develops vomiting, lethargy, and slowed responses after a dose increase. She has eaten little for a week because of nausea. Examination shows asterixis without focal weakness. Glucose and sodium are normal, liver aminotransferases and bilirubin are normal, and serum ammonia is markedly elevated. EEG shows generalized slowing without seizures. What best explains this deterioration?

options.text: Nonconvulsive status established by generalized EEG slowing
options.explanation: Generalized slowing indicates diffuse dysfunction and is not equivalent to an ictal pattern; the described EEG provides no evidence of ongoing seizures.

options.text: Isolated dietary protein excess requiring permanent protein elimination
options.explanation: The patient has poor intake rather than protein excess, and permanent protein elimination could worsen malnutrition without addressing the medication-associated disturbance.

options.text: Valproate-associated hyperammonemic encephalopathy
options.explanation: Valproate can disrupt ammonia handling, sometimes involving carnitine depletion; encephalopathy may occur despite normal hepatic biochemical tests and a therapeutic drug concentration.

options.text: Acute hepatic failure proven by the ammonia result
options.explanation: Ammonia elevation alone does not prove hepatic failure; the medication exposure and absence of reported hepatic injury favor a drug-associated process.

explanation: Valproate-associated hyperammonemic encephalopathy should be considered when a patient develops cognitive slowing, vomiting, or reduced consciousness during treatment. Normal aminotransferases do not exclude it. Effects on urea-cycle metabolism and carnitine availability can contribute, and nutritional depletion increases concern. Management requires urgent clinical assessment, interruption of the offending drug when appropriate, seizure coverage, and consideration of levocarnitine with specialist or toxicology input. The question asks for the unifying diagnosis, not a fixed antidote dose; an underlying urea-cycle disorder may need investigation in severe or recurrent cases.
objective: Recognize valproate-related hyperammonemic encephalopathy despite normal liver tests, particularly with nutritional depletion.
keyPoints: Ammonia elevation does not by itself diagnose hepatic failure.
Review drug and nutritional contributors to encephalopathy.

subject: Neurology
stem: A 29-year-old woman underwent gastric bypass seven weeks ago and has vomited almost daily for three weeks. She now needs support to walk and cannot follow a conversation. Examination shows horizontal nystagmus and impaired abduction of both eyes. Glucose is 91 mg/dL, and CT shows no hemorrhage. She does not drink alcohol. Which intervention should begin immediately while additional evaluation proceeds?

options.text: Exclude a vitamin disorder because alcohol use is absent
options.explanation: Thiamine depletion also occurs with vomiting, malabsorption, starvation, and bariatric surgery; alcohol exposure is neither required nor sufficient for diagnosis.

options.text: Administer parenteral thiamine
options.explanation: Prolonged vomiting after bariatric surgery can rapidly deplete thiamine, and the ocular, gait, and cognitive findings warrant immediate parenteral treatment.

options.text: Wait for a serum thiamine level before treatment
options.explanation: Laboratory confirmation can be delayed or unreliable and should not postpone treatment when suspected thiamine-related neurological injury may become irreversible.

options.text: Give folate alone and arrange routine clinic follow-up
options.explanation: Folate addresses a different nutritional pathway and does not treat this acute ocular, cerebellar, and cognitive syndrome requiring urgent monitored care.

explanation: The clinical pattern suggests Wernicke encephalopathy caused by thiamine depletion after prolonged postoperative vomiting. Alcohol use is not required. Prompt parenteral replacement is appropriate because oral absorption and intake may be inadequate and neurological injury can become permanent. Magnesium and other nutritional or electrolyte deficiencies should also be assessed, and the cause of vomiting investigated. If hypoglycemia were present, emergency glucose should not be delayed; thiamine should be given promptly alongside treatment. A normal CT does not exclude this metabolic neurological condition.
objective: Treat suspected Wernicke encephalopathy promptly in a vomiting postbariatric patient regardless of alcohol history.
keyPoints: Bariatric vomiting is a thiamine-risk history.
Do not delay emergency glucose for thiamine when hypoglycemia is present.

subject: Neurology
stem: A 68-year-old man develops progressive imbalance and hand tingling over six months. Vibration and position sense are reduced in his feet, and knee reflexes are brisk. Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL and the neutrophil count is low. Vitamin B12 and methylmalonic acid are normal. He has taken high-dose zinc tablets daily for two years to prevent colds. Which additional measurement most directly evaluates the suspected cause?

options.text: Serum copper with ceruloplasmin
options.explanation: Excess zinc impairs copper absorption, and copper depletion can combine a posterior-column myeloneuropathy with anemia and neutropenia resembling other neurological deficiencies.

options.text: Serum iron as the only additional nutritional investigation
options.explanation: Iron deficiency can cause anemia but does not adequately explain combined myelopathy and neutropenia in the setting of sustained excessive zinc exposure.

options.text: Serum calcium to establish an acute tetany syndrome
options.explanation: Acute hypocalcemia causes neuromuscular irritability rather than this slowly progressive sensory ataxia with cytopenias and a specific competing mineral exposure.

options.text: Serum folate to prove all neurological deficiency syndromes
options.explanation: Folate deficiency can cause macrocytic anemia but does not typically explain this posterior-column syndrome, and it cannot substitute for evaluating copper.

explanation: Copper deficiency is an important acquired mimic of subacute combined degeneration. Prolonged high zinc intake can reduce intestinal copper absorption, and neurological findings may coexist with anemia and neutropenia. Normal B12 and methylmalonic acid make B12 deficiency less likely in this vignette without excluding every alternative diagnosis. Serum copper and ceruloplasmin help evaluate the suspected depletion, although both require interpretation in context. Stopping unnecessary zinc and replacing copper under supervision can arrest progression; neurological recovery may be incomplete, making timely recognition important.
objective: Investigate copper deficiency when chronic zinc exposure accompanies sensory myelopathy and cytopenias.
keyPoints: Ask specifically about over-the-counter mineral products.
Nutritional myelopathy may accompany marrow abnormalities.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: A 47-year-old woman has gradually worsening burning feet and imbalance. Glucose testing, kidney function, B12, and thyroid studies are normal. She takes an energy powder, a magnesium product, and a B-complex tablet; review shows that all contain pyridoxine and her combined intake is markedly above the recommended daily amount. Examination reveals distal sensory loss without weakness. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Double the B-complex dose to regenerate peripheral nerves
options.explanation: More pyridoxine can worsen a toxicity-related neuropathy, and an unselected vitamin escalation ignores the excessive exposure already identified during reconciliation.

options.text: Reassure her that water-soluble vitamins cannot cause toxicity
options.explanation: Water solubility does not guarantee safety at supplemental doses; pyridoxine is a recognized cause of sensory neurological injury with excess exposure.

options.text: Start immunosuppression solely on the basis of burning pain
options.explanation: Burning pain is nonspecific and does not establish immune neuropathy; an identifiable potentially toxic supplement exposure should be addressed first.

options.text: Stop excessive pyridoxine exposure and reassess the neuropathy
options.explanation: Cumulative vitamin B6 exposure from several products can cause sensory neuropathy; removing the suspected excess is appropriate while evaluating other causes.

explanation: Supplement reconciliation must include the total amount of each ingredient across products. Pyridoxine excess can produce predominantly sensory neuropathy and imbalance; taking several apparently different supplements can create an unrecognized cumulative dose. The appropriate action is to remove unnecessary excessive exposure, assess severity, and follow neurological function while continuing an appropriate differential evaluation. Recovery may be gradual and incomplete. This case does not establish a single universal toxic threshold because susceptibility and duration vary, and regional regulatory intake limits are not identical.
objective: Recognize cumulative pyridoxine exposure as a reversible contributor to sensory neuropathy and stop the excess.
keyPoints: Count ingredients across all supplements.
Water-soluble does not mean harmless at high intake.

subject: Neurology
stem: A 66-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes treated with metformin for twelve years reports new numbness and difficulty walking in the dark. Her glycated hemoglobin has remained near 6.7%, and she has no retinopathy. Examination shows reduced vibration in the feet. Hemoglobin is 11.1 g/dL with a mean corpuscular volume of 104 fL. She eats a varied diet. Which test is most appropriate next?

options.text: Serum albumin alone to exclude all micronutrient deficiencies
options.explanation: Albumin reflects multiple nonnutritional influences and can be normal despite B12 deficiency; it does not evaluate this specific neurological and hematological pattern.

options.text: A fasting insulin level to determine the nerve lesion location
options.explanation: Insulin concentration does not establish the cause or localization of this sensory deficit and would not investigate the associated macrocytosis.

options.text: Serum vitamin B12, with a functional marker if the result is indeterminate
options.explanation: Long-term metformin exposure, macrocytosis, and sensory dysfunction justify evaluating a potentially treatable B12 deficiency even when dietary intake appears adequate.

options.text: No testing because diabetes fully explains every sensory complaint
options.explanation: Diabetes is common but does not eliminate additional causes; macrocytosis and prolonged metformin exposure specifically warrant evaluation for a nutritional contributor.

explanation: Metformin can reduce B12 absorption during long-term treatment. New sensory symptoms accompanied by macrocytosis should therefore prompt B12 evaluation rather than automatic attribution to diabetic neuropathy. A borderline serum value may require methylmalonic acid or another appropriate functional assessment, interpreted with renal function. A varied diet does not exclude impaired absorption. If clinically significant neurological deficiency is suspected, evaluation and treatment should proceed promptly rather than waiting for advanced anemia. The aim is to identify an additional modifiable contributor while maintaining appropriate diabetes care.
objective: Assess B12 status in long-term metformin users with new neuropathic symptoms or macrocytosis.
keyPoints: Dietary adequacy does not exclude impaired absorption.
Diabetes and nutritional neuropathy can coexist.

subject: Biochemistry
stem: A 42-year-old man with severe food insecurity has eaten mainly sweetened tea and crackers for two months. He presents with confusion and gait instability. Lactate remains elevated despite restoration of normal blood pressure, oxygenation, and intravascular volume; cultures reveal no infection. Neurological findings improve after parenteral thiamine. Impaired activity of which enzyme most directly explains the diversion of pyruvate toward lactate before treatment?

options.text: Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
options.explanation: This enzyme also requires thiamine, but it acts within the citric acid cycle rather than directly converting pyruvate into acetyl-CoA at the specified branch point.

options.text: Pyruvate dehydrogenase
options.explanation: Thiamine pyrophosphate is a required cofactor for this complex, so deficiency reduces entry of pyruvate carbon into oxidative acetyl-CoA metabolism.

options.text: Lactate dehydrogenase
options.explanation: This enzyme converts pyruvate to lactate and remains available during thiamine depletion; its increased flux is the consequence rather than the deficient step.

options.text: Glucose-6-phosphatase
options.explanation: This gluconeogenic enzyme releases free glucose and is not the thiamine-dependent mitochondrial link between glycolytic pyruvate and acetyl-CoA formation.

explanation: Thiamine pyrophosphate participates in several reactions, including the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex. Without adequate cofactor, pyruvate is less effectively converted to acetyl-CoA and is diverted toward lactate regeneration of NAD+. Consequently, nutritional deficiency can contribute to elevated lactate even when oxygen delivery and circulation have been corrected. The dietary history and neurological response support this mechanism, but elevated lactate still demands evaluation for sepsis, ischemia, medication effects, and other causes. Thiamine treatment does not remove the need to identify the broader cause of malnutrition.
objective: Connect thiamine depletion with impaired pyruvate oxidation and a potentially nonhypoxic contribution to lactate elevation.
keyPoints: Lactate elevation has causes beyond tissue hypoxia.
Micronutrient replacement complements evaluation of nutritional deprivation.

subject: Neurology
stem: A 38-year-old man with long-standing pancreatic insufficiency reports worsening balance and difficulty using stairs in dim light. He often skips pancreatic enzymes because of cost and has bulky oily stools. Examination shows absent ankle reflexes, impaired vibration, and limb dysmetria. Vitamin B12 and methylmalonic acid are normal. Which deficiency should be investigated as a potentially treatable contributor to his neurological symptoms?

options.text: Vitamin E
options.explanation: Fat malabsorption can reduce vitamin E uptake, and depletion may cause peripheral neuropathy, impaired proprioception, and ataxia resembling inherited neurological disorders.

options.text: Vitamin C
options.explanation: Vitamin C deficiency chiefly causes connective-tissue manifestations such as gingival bleeding and bruising rather than the combined sensory and coordination deficits described.

options.text: Vitamin K
options.explanation: Vitamin K deficiency may accompany fat malabsorption but principally impairs coagulation; it does not usually produce this progressive sensory ataxia syndrome.

options.text: Folate
options.explanation: Folate depletion can contribute to macrocytic anemia, but it does not characteristically cause this posterior-column and peripheral neurological phenotype with chronic fat malabsorption.

explanation: Vitamin E is absorbed with fat, making chronic pancreatic insufficiency and inadequate enzyme treatment important risk factors for depletion. Deficiency can affect peripheral nerves and sensory pathways, producing areflexia, loss of position or vibration sense, and ataxia. Testing and replacement require interpretation alongside lipid status and the underlying malabsorptive disease. Improving access to pancreatic enzyme treatment addresses an ongoing cause rather than merely replacing one vitamin. The neurological pattern also warrants consideration of B12, copper, hereditary ataxias, and other causes when the course or response is atypical.
objective: Consider vitamin E depletion in sensory ataxia associated with chronic fat malabsorption.
keyPoints: Address the cause of malabsorption alongside replacement.
A normal B12 result does not exclude other nutritional neurological disease.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: A 71-year-old man with Parkinson disease takes carbidopa-levodopa on a stable schedule. His morning dose works predictably, but the lunch dose often has little effect since he began drinking a large protein supplement with lunch. His weight is low and the dietitian wants to preserve total daily protein intake. Which mechanism best explains the meal-associated decline in response?

options.text: Irreversible destruction of dopamine receptors by dietary protein
options.explanation: Dietary protein does not irreversibly destroy dopamine receptors; this reproducible timing pattern is more consistent with a transport or absorption interaction.

options.text: Chelation of levodopa by dietary glucose
options.explanation: The reported change involves a protein supplement, and glucose chelation does not explain competition at amino-acid transport pathways relevant to levodopa.

options.text: Complete conversion of carbidopa into dietary amino acids
options.explanation: Carbidopa inhibits peripheral decarboxylation; it is not consumed by conversion into amino acids when a patient eats a protein-rich meal.

options.text: Competition between levodopa and large neutral amino acids for transport
options.explanation: Levodopa shares transport pathways with dietary amino acids, so a large protein load can reduce or delay its clinical availability in susceptible patients.

explanation: Levodopa resembles a large neutral amino acid and can compete with dietary amino acids during intestinal and blood-brain transport. A protein-associated fluctuation is therefore plausible when symptoms correlate reproducibly with a large supplement. Management can include individualized medication timing or redistribution of protein across the day, while maintaining adequate overall nutrition. This is particularly important in an underweight patient; indiscriminate protein restriction would be harmful. Other explanations for fluctuations, including gastric emptying, adherence, and progression, still require review before attributing every off period to meals.
objective: Explain protein-associated levodopa fluctuations without recommending nutritionally unsafe global protein restriction.
keyPoints: Meal composition can influence drug response.
Preserve total nutritional adequacy when adjusting timing.

subject: Neurology
stem: A 46-year-old woman reports an evening urge to move her legs that begins while sitting and improves when she walks. There is no weakness, sensory loss, or leg swelling. She has heavy menstrual bleeding and eats little iron-rich food. Hemoglobin is 12.6 g/dL, ferritin is 14 ng/mL, and transferrin saturation is low. Which component should be included in the initial management plan?

options.text: Prescribe escalating dopamine agonists without addressing iron depletion
options.explanation: Symptom drugs do not correct the demonstrated deficiency, and some dopaminergic strategies carry augmentation risks that require consideration in current guidance.

options.text: Recommend strict bed rest whenever symptoms occur
options.explanation: Symptoms characteristically improve with movement; bed rest does not replace evaluation and treatment of the iron depletion or other provoking factors.

options.text: Replace depleted iron stores and evaluate the source of iron loss
options.explanation: Typical restless legs with clearly depleted iron stores warrants iron repletion and investigation of ongoing loss even when hemoglobin remains normal.

options.text: Withhold iron because the hemoglobin is within the laboratory range
options.explanation: Iron depletion can precede anemia, and iron-store assessment is relevant to restless legs rather than being determined solely by hemoglobin concentration.

explanation: The timing, urge to move, worsening at rest, and relief with activity support restless legs syndrome. Markedly low ferritin and transferrin saturation identify a modifiable contributor even before overt anemia appears. Replacement should be individualized to tolerance, absorption, degree of depletion, and contemporary guidance, while menstrual blood loss and dietary adequacy are evaluated. Medication review and aggravating factors also matter. This question uses unequivocally low stores and avoids relying on a disputed borderline cutoff; iron treatment should still be monitored rather than continued indefinitely without reassessment.
objective: Include iron repletion and evaluation of iron loss in restless legs syndrome with clearly depleted stores despite normal hemoglobin.
keyPoints: Normal hemoglobin does not establish iron sufficiency.
Investigate why stores are depleted.

subject: Neurology
stem: A 52-year-old man develops diplopia, dry mouth, dysarthria, and symmetric descending weakness after sharing home-preserved vegetables. His spouse has similar symptoms. He is afebrile and alert, with dilated poorly reactive pupils and no sensory loss. Respiratory strength is declining, and airway support is being arranged. What additional action should occur immediately while diagnostic specimens are collected?

options.text: Administer high-dose corticosteroids as the only disease-specific therapy
options.explanation: Corticosteroids do not neutralize the toxin and are not a substitute for prompt antitoxin assessment, respiratory support, and public-health involvement.

options.text: Contact public health for emergency botulism consultation and antitoxin
options.explanation: The exposure cluster and cranial-to-descending paralysis are highly concerning for botulism; early antitoxin can limit further toxin-mediated injury and should not await confirmation.

options.text: Wait for a stool toxin result before requesting antitoxin
options.explanation: Laboratory confirmation may take time, while unbound toxin can continue causing paralysis; delaying consultation sacrifices the opportunity for earlier neutralization.

options.text: Give a cholinesterase inhibitor as definitive treatment
options.explanation: This does not neutralize circulating botulinum toxin and is not definitive therapy for foodborne botulism with progressive respiratory weakness.

explanation: Foodborne botulism produces an acute afebrile syndrome of cranial neuropathies followed by symmetric descending weakness, often with autonomic signs and preserved sensation. Multiple affected diners strengthen the exposure link. Respiratory stabilization is essential, and emergency consultation through public-health channels facilitates antitoxin assessment. Antitoxin neutralizes circulating toxin but does not reverse toxin already bound to nerve terminals, explaining why treatment should not wait for laboratory proof. Specimen collection remains important, but logistics should be coordinated so they do not delay needed treatment.
objective: Arrange emergency antitoxin consultation for clinically suspected foodborne botulism without waiting for confirmatory toxin testing.
keyPoints: Antitoxin prevents additional injury rather than instantly reversing established paralysis.
Support ventilation and involve public health promptly.

subject: Neurology
stem: A previously healthy 7-year-old girl develops an unsteady gait and progressive leg weakness during a camping trip. She is afebrile, alert, and has absent leg reflexes without sensory loss. Careful scalp examination finds an engorged attached tick. The tick is removed, respiratory strength is monitored, and substantial improvement begins over the next day. Which diagnosis best explains the complete course?

options.text: Tick paralysis
options.explanation: A toxin-associated paralysis can cause acute areflexic weakness during tick attachment and improve after removal, fitting the exposure and recovery trajectory.

options.text: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy
options.explanation: A chronic immune neuropathy usually evolves over a longer interval and would not be expected to improve promptly simply after tick removal.

options.text: Acute transverse myelitis
options.explanation: A spinal cord syndrome generally includes a sensory level, autonomic dysfunction, or evolving upper motor signs rather than this exposure-linked rapidly reversible pattern.

options.text: Duchenne muscular dystrophy
options.explanation: Duchenne disease causes progressive childhood muscle weakness over years and does not produce sudden areflexic paralysis with rapid recovery after an exposure ends.

explanation: Tick paralysis belongs in the differential of acute flaccid weakness, particularly after outdoor exposure. A meticulous skin and scalp examination can identify an attached tick that is easy to miss. Improvement after removal supports the diagnosis, although speed and severity vary by tick species and region; respiratory deterioration can still occur and monitoring is needed. Guillain-Barre syndrome and other neurological emergencies should remain under consideration when recovery is not as expected. The decisive clue is the exposure-linked course rather than areflexia alone.
objective: Recognize tick paralysis from an attached tick and exposure-linked recovery while preserving respiratory monitoring.
keyPoints: Examine the scalp in acute flaccid weakness after camping.
Tick species and geography influence the course.

subject: Neurology
stem: A 40-year-old man has confirmed Guillain-Barre syndrome after a diarrheal illness. Within four days he progresses from walking unaided to being unable to stand. He is admitted for respiratory and autonomic monitoring; renal function and hemodynamics are stable. The team discusses disease-modifying therapy. Which treatment is an accepted option for this degree of rapidly progressive functional impairment?

options.text: Oral prednisone as the sole disease-modifying treatment
options.explanation: Corticosteroid monotherapy has not shown the expected benefit in Guillain-Barre syndrome and should not replace established immunotherapy for rapidly progressive nonambulatory disease.

options.text: Levodopa to restore peripheral motor transmission
options.explanation: Levodopa treats selected central dopaminergic motor disorders and does not address the acute immune-mediated peripheral nerve injury causing this patient's weakness.

options.text: Observation without immunotherapy until weakness has lasted months
options.explanation: Waiting for a chronic course misses the early treatment opportunity in rapidly progressive disease and exposes the patient to additional disability and respiratory risk.

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin
options.explanation: IVIG is an accepted disease-specific treatment for significant acute Guillain-Barre syndrome; plasma exchange is another effective option selected according to clinical circumstances.

explanation: The question begins after diagnostic confirmation and focuses on treatment rather than recognition of the classic syndrome. Rapid progression to inability to walk is a strong reason to initiate accepted immunotherapy, commonly IVIG or plasma exchange. These are alternatives, not automatically a combined sequence. Respiratory mechanics, bulbar function, autonomic instability, thrombosis prevention, pain, and rehabilitation require ongoing attention regardless of treatment choice. Corticosteroids should not be extrapolated from other inflammatory neurological disorders as effective monotherapy for Guillain-Barre syndrome.
objective: Select established immunotherapy for rapidly progressive nonambulatory Guillain-Barre syndrome rather than corticosteroid monotherapy.
keyPoints: IVIG and plasma exchange are accepted alternatives.
Immunotherapy does not replace respiratory or autonomic monitoring.

subject: Neurology
stem: A 64-year-old man with a long smoking history has difficulty rising from a chair and persistent dry mouth. Knee reflexes are initially absent but become detectable after repeated quadriceps contraction. Sensation is normal. Nerve stimulation shows a marked increment in compound muscle action potential after exercise. Which associated condition should be actively investigated as part of his evaluation?

options.text: Colon adenocarcinoma as the established explanation for this electrophysiology
options.explanation: Routine age-appropriate colorectal care remains relevant, but this specific neuromuscular syndrome and smoking history particularly raise concern for small-cell lung carcinoma.

options.text: Renal cell carcinoma as the characteristic paraneoplastic association
options.explanation: Renal tumors can produce paraneoplastic effects, but the specific presynaptic junction syndrome described is particularly associated with small-cell lung carcinoma rather than renal cell carcinoma.

options.text: Small-cell lung carcinoma
options.explanation: A presynaptic Lambert-Eaton pattern can be paraneoplastic, particularly with small-cell lung carcinoma, making malignancy evaluation important in this high-risk patient.

options.text: Thymoma as the characteristic association of every junction disorder
options.explanation: Thymoma is associated with myasthenia gravis; the facilitating reflexes, autonomic features, and incremental response here instead indicate a presynaptic syndrome.

explanation: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome results from impaired presynaptic transmitter release, often involving antibodies against voltage-gated calcium channels. Proximal weakness, autonomic symptoms, reduced reflexes, and facilitation after activity distinguish it from many postsynaptic or neuropathic disorders. The syndrome can precede discovery of an underlying malignancy, especially small-cell lung carcinoma. Investigation should follow a specialist-directed strategy and may need reassessment if an initial screen is negative. This question does not assume every affected patient has cancer; it identifies an association important enough to investigate.
objective: Investigate small-cell lung carcinoma when a clinical and electrophysiological Lambert-Eaton pattern is identified.
keyPoints: Facilitation helps distinguish presynaptic junction disease.
Paraneoplastic symptoms can precede tumor detection.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: A 55-year-old woman with established myasthenia gravis undergoes abdominal surgery. She had mild residual diplopia before surgery. After receiving intravenous magnesium for an electrolyte abnormality, she develops increased ptosis and weak cough. Oxygen and ventilatory assessment are initiated, and the team reviews potentially aggravating medications. Which effect of magnesium most directly contributes to worsening neuromuscular transmission in this susceptible patient?

options.text: Increased acetylcholine vesicle exocytosis at the motor terminal
options.explanation: Increased release would not explain the reduced junctional reserve described; magnesium instead can reduce calcium-dependent presynaptic release and worsen transmission in myasthenia.

options.text: Reduction of presynaptic calcium-dependent acetylcholine release
options.explanation: Magnesium can impair calcium-dependent transmitter release, reducing the safety margin of neuromuscular transmission that is already compromised in myasthenia gravis.

options.text: Irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic cleft
options.explanation: Magnesium is not an irreversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor; the relevant aggravating effect is reduced transmitter release rather than prolonged acetylcholine persistence.

options.text: Irreversible binding of magnesium to postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors
options.explanation: The relevant effect is inhibition of calcium-dependent transmitter release, not an irreversible postsynaptic receptor-binding mechanism that permanently prevents acetylcholine action at the end plate.

explanation: Patients with myasthenia have reduced postsynaptic neuromuscular reserve. Magnesium can further weaken transmission by interfering with presynaptic calcium-dependent acetylcholine release, and clinically necessary replacement should therefore be individualized and monitored. New bulbar or respiratory weakness requires urgent assessment regardless of pulse oximetry, which can remain normal early in hypoventilation. Perioperative illness, anesthetic drugs, and other medications are additional possible contributors. The mechanistic question does not imply that every magnesium exposure is prohibited or that this temporal association alone proves causality.
objective: Explain why magnesium can worsen weakness in patients with compromised neuromuscular junction reserve.
keyPoints: Review perioperative drugs when myasthenic weakness worsens.
Respiratory mechanics matter before oxygen saturation falls.

subject: Neurology
stem: A 58-year-old woman with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis has lost 8% of her weight in three months. Meals now take ninety minutes, and she often stops because chewing is exhausting. Dietitian-guided supplements have not restored intake. Her respiratory function has begun to decline, but she communicates clearly and wants to continue disease-directed supportive care. What is the most appropriate next step in nutritional planning?

options.text: Discuss gastrostomy benefits, burdens, timing, and alternatives now with the multidisciplinary team
options.explanation: Persistent nutritional decline despite oral strategies warrants timely shared planning, including assessment of respiratory and procedural risks before a feeding emergency develops.

options.text: Wait until she cannot communicate before discussing tube feeding
options.explanation: Delaying removes opportunities for informed participation and may increase procedural complexity as respiratory impairment and nutritional depletion progress.

options.text: Promise that gastrostomy will prevent all aspiration and reverse ALS
options.explanation: A feeding tube can support intake but does not cure motor neuron degeneration or eliminate aspiration from secretions and reflux.

options.text: Require tube placement regardless of her goals because weight has fallen
options.explanation: Nutritional risk supports a recommendation and informed discussion, not overriding a capable patient's values or treating the procedure as compulsory.

explanation: ALS-related bulbar dysfunction and meal fatigue can cause significant weight loss before complete loss of oral intake. Gastrostomy may supplement rather than automatically replace every oral pleasure, depending on swallowing safety. It does not abolish aspiration risk or reverse ALS. The central decision is early informed planning, not a rigid universal lung-function threshold or forced intervention.
objective: Initiate shared enteral-feeding planning when ALS causes persistent weight loss despite optimized oral intake.

Tube feeding supports nutrition but does not eliminate aspiration or cure ALS.

subject: Neurology
stem: A 76-year-old man arrives ninety minutes after sudden aphasia and right hemiplegia. CT excludes hemorrhage, and CT angiography shows a proximal left middle cerebral artery occlusion. Imaging shows a small established infarct. He took apixaban two hours earlier, and the local stroke protocol does not permit intravenous thrombolysis with his current anticoagulant exposure. What should the team do next?

options.text: Exclude every reperfusion procedure because apixaban was taken
options.explanation: Intravenous thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy have different selection issues; anticoagulant exposure alone should not end assessment for a treatable large-vessel occlusion.

options.text: Delay vascular treatment until an outpatient anticoagulation appointment
options.explanation: Large-vessel ischemic stroke is time-sensitive, and outpatient review cannot substitute for urgent assessment of reperfusion options and organized stroke care.

options.text: Give additional apixaban to dissolve the intracranial clot immediately
options.explanation: Apixaban is not an acute clot-dissolving therapy, and extra dosing does not replace mechanical reperfusion assessment while potentially increasing bleeding risk.

options.text: Arrange immediate endovascular thrombectomy assessment
options.explanation: A proximal occlusion with limited established injury warrants urgent thrombectomy evaluation; inability to receive intravenous thrombolysis does not automatically eliminate endovascular treatment.

explanation: The stem establishes a disabling proximal arterial occlusion, early presentation, and a relatively small established infarct. These findings justify immediate evaluation by an endovascular stroke team. Intravenous thrombolysis eligibility and thrombectomy eligibility must be assessed separately; a contraindication to the former does not automatically prohibit the latter. Exact thrombectomy selection depends on imaging, vessel anatomy, baseline function, timing, and contemporary protocols. Additional anticoagulant dosing is not a substitute for reperfusion. Transfer logistics should be coordinated promptly if the presenting center lacks endovascular capability.
objective: Continue urgent thrombectomy assessment for a suitable large-vessel stroke even when recent anticoagulation precludes intravenous thrombolysis under the applicable protocol.
keyPoints: Assess reperfusion modalities separately.
Do not let one exclusion end all acute stroke treatment pathways.

subject: Neurology
stem: A 39-year-old man develops left-sided neck pain after a vigorous climbing session. The next morning his spouse notices a smaller left pupil and mild left eyelid droop. Sweating is preserved, extraocular movements are intact, and strength is normal. He has never had these findings before. Which diagnosis most urgently needs evaluation with appropriate head and neck vascular imaging?

options.text: Posterior communicating artery aneurysm causing a complete third nerve palsy
options.explanation: A compressive third nerve palsy more typically produces a dilated pupil and extraocular movement deficits, whereas this pupil is smaller and movements are intact.

options.text: Myasthenia gravis limited to the eyelid
options.explanation: Myasthenia can cause ptosis but does not typically produce a small pupil or a painful neck syndrome involving sympathetic pathway dysfunction.

options.text: Internal carotid artery dissection
options.explanation: Painful partial Horner syndrome can result from injury to sympathetic fibers adjacent to the internal carotid artery and may precede ischemic neurological deficits.

options.text: Uncomplicated trapezius strain explaining the entire presentation
options.explanation: Muscle strain may cause neck pain but does not account for a new ipsilateral pupillary abnormality and ptosis requiring vascular evaluation.

explanation: The sympathetic fibers accompanying the internal carotid artery can be affected by dissection, producing ipsilateral ptosis and miosis, sometimes without facial anhidrosis. New unilateral neck or head pain makes the combination particularly concerning even before a focal ischemic deficit appears. Dedicated vascular imaging evaluates the arterial wall and lumen. The absence of weakness does not make this benign. Neck muscle pain and ocular disorders remain alternatives, but neither explains all findings as coherently. Management after confirmation depends on vascular anatomy, ischemic symptoms, and specialist review.
objective: Recognize painful partial Horner syndrome as a possible carotid dissection requiring urgent vascular evaluation.
keyPoints: Dissection may present before stroke.
A small pupil helps distinguish Horner syndrome from a compressive third nerve palsy.

subject: Neurology
stem: A 57-year-old man receiving antibiotics for Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia develops severe focal thoracic back pain. He is now afebrile. Over six hours, his legs become weak and he develops urinary retention. Examination reveals reduced pin sensation below the umbilicus and brisk knee reflexes. Plain spinal radiographs show degenerative changes only. Which investigation is most appropriate urgently?

options.text: No further investigation because antibiotics eliminated the fever
options.explanation: Antibiotics can suppress fever without excluding a focal collection or mechanical compression; new neurological deficits require urgent reassessment despite apparent systemic improvement.

options.text: Contrast-enhanced MRI of the relevant spine with urgent specialist involvement
options.explanation: Bacteremia, severe focal spinal pain, and an evolving cord syndrome raise concern for epidural infection with compression, which requires urgent MRI and specialist assessment.

options.text: Repeat plain radiographs in several weeks
options.explanation: Plain films do not adequately assess epidural soft tissue or cord compression, and waiting risks permanent injury during an evolving neurological emergency.

options.text: Outpatient nerve conduction testing of both legs
options.explanation: Peripheral testing cannot rapidly assess a thoracic compressive lesion, and a sensory level with urinary retention points toward a spinal cord process.

explanation: Spinal epidural infection can progress to cord compression, and the complete triad of fever, back pain, and neurological deficit is not required. Existing bacteremia and focal pain markedly increase concern; evolving weakness, a sensory level, and bladder dysfunction establish urgency. MRI evaluates the epidural space, vertebrae, and neural structures more effectively than plain radiographs. Antibiotic management and neurosurgical evaluation should proceed urgently according to stability and imaging findings. This is distinct from routine mechanical back pain and should not be deferred because fever has improved.
objective: Obtain urgent spinal MRI for a progressive cord syndrome during bacteremia even when the patient is afebrile and radiographs are unrevealing.
keyPoints: Absence of the classic triad does not exclude spinal epidural infection.
Treat new cord dysfunction as time-sensitive.

subject: Neurology
stem: After repair of a thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm, a 69-year-old man awakens with bilateral leg paralysis. Pain and temperature sensation are absent below the lower chest, but toe position and vibration remain detectable. His arms and cranial nerve examination are normal. Urgent imaging is arranged to evaluate a spinal complication. Which vascular territory best fits the selective neurological pattern?

options.text: Anterior spinal artery territory
options.explanation: The anterior cord includes corticospinal and spinothalamic pathways, while dorsal-column function may be relatively preserved when posterior spinal circulation remains intact.

options.text: Posterior spinal artery territory alone
options.explanation: An isolated posterior territory lesion would primarily impair position and vibration sense, which are specifically preserved in this postoperative sensory pattern.

options.text: Bilateral posterior cerebral artery territories
options.explanation: Posterior cerebral ischemia affects cerebral structures, often including vision, and does not explain a thoracic sensory level with selective spinal modality loss.

options.text: A single common fibular nerve territory
options.explanation: One peripheral nerve lesion cannot explain bilateral paralysis, a truncal sensory level, and selective loss of pain and temperature across both legs.

explanation: Aortic procedures can compromise blood supply to the spinal cord. Weakness together with loss of pain and temperature below a level, while vibration and position sense remain relatively spared, localizes to the anterior cord. Corticospinal and spinothalamic pathways are affected, whereas dorsal columns are supplied mainly by posterior spinal circulation. Actual infarct patterns can be incomplete or mixed, so this physiological localization is not a substitute for urgent postoperative evaluation and treatment. Peripheral nerve injury and cerebral stroke do not match the sensory level or modality pattern.
objective: Localize postoperative weakness with pain-temperature loss and preserved proprioception to the anterior spinal circulation.
keyPoints: Selective sensory modalities help localize cord injury.
Postaortic neurological deficits need urgent assessment.

subject: Neurology
stem: A 67-year-old woman presents with abrupt vomiting, severe occipital pain, and inability to stand. CT reveals a cerebellar hemorrhage compressing the fourth ventricle with enlarging lateral ventricles. She was independently alert before symptom onset. During monitoring she becomes progressively somnolent. Blood pressure treatment and airway preparation are underway. Which additional action has the highest priority?

options.text: Arrange routine outpatient balance rehabilitation before consultation
options.explanation: Rehabilitation is relevant after stabilization but cannot treat acute posterior fossa mass effect or an obstructed ventricular system causing deteriorating consciousness.

options.text: Administer an oral vestibular suppressant and observe overnight
options.explanation: Symptom suppression does not relieve mechanical compression, and oral treatment is unsafe in a progressively somnolent patient with an evolving neurological emergency.

options.text: Perform lumbar puncture to lower pressure before specialist review
options.explanation: A posterior fossa mass with hydrocephalus makes lumbar cerebrospinal fluid removal hazardous because it can worsen pressure gradients and precipitate herniation.

options.text: Obtain immediate neurosurgical evaluation for decompression and management of hydrocephalus
options.explanation: Posterior fossa hemorrhage with obstructed cerebrospinal fluid flow and declining consciousness can rapidly cause fatal compression and requires urgent neurosurgical assessment.

explanation: The posterior fossa has limited space, and cerebellar hemorrhage can compress the brainstem or obstruct the fourth ventricle. Deteriorating consciousness and hydrocephalus are urgent warning signs requiring neurosurgical evaluation rather than symptom treatment alone. Airway and physiological stabilization continue concurrently. Definitive decisions may involve hematoma evacuation, decompression, and cerebrospinal fluid diversion under specialist judgment. Lumbar puncture does not safely address an obstructed cranial compartment. The question intentionally emphasizes the combination of deterioration and obstructive anatomy rather than asserting a universal size-only surgical rule.
objective: Escalate cerebellar hemorrhage with obstructive hydrocephalus and declining consciousness to urgent neurosurgical care.
keyPoints: Posterior fossa lesions can deteriorate quickly.

subject: Neurology
stem: Seven days after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage treated by coiling, a 48-year-old woman develops new expressive language difficulty and right arm drift. Earlier examinations had been stable, and she has received no new sedatives. Glucose, sodium, temperature, and oxygenation are normal. Repeat CT shows no new blood and no hydrocephalus. Which complication is the leading concern requiring urgent vascular and perfusion assessment?

options.text: Normal recovery from coiling requiring no reassessment
options.explanation: A new focal neurological change after previous stability is not an expected harmless milestone and requires urgent evaluation for treatable intracranial complications.

options.text: Hyponatremic encephalopathy established by the time interval alone
options.explanation: The sodium is normal, and a focal language-motor syndrome should not be attributed to a metabolic complication without supporting laboratory evidence.

options.text: Delayed cerebral ischemia associated with posthemorrhagic vascular dysfunction
options.explanation: A new focal deficit several days after subarachnoid hemorrhage without rebleeding or hydrocephalus raises concern for delayed ischemia, often associated with vasospasm.

options.text: A remote stable peripheral neuropathy
options.explanation: A peripheral neuropathy does not explain newly impaired language together with unilateral arm drift emerging during the recognized delayed complication period.

explanation: Delayed cerebral ischemia is a major complication after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage and can appear after the initial bleeding has been secured. The deficit may reflect vascular narrowing and additional microcirculatory mechanisms; angiographic vasospasm and clinical ischemia are related but not identical concepts. New focal symptoms warrant urgent reassessment while excluding rebleeding, hydrocephalus, seizures, metabolic derangements, and infection. Normal CT for new hemorrhage does not exclude ischemia. Specialized monitoring and management depend on neurological examination, hemodynamics, and vascular or perfusion findings.
objective: Suspect delayed cerebral ischemia when a new focal deficit develops days after stabilized aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage.
keyPoints: Securing the aneurysm does not eliminate delayed complications.
Angiographic vasospasm and clinical ischemia are not interchangeable.

subject: Neurology
stem: A 54-year-old woman develops sudden left retro-orbital pain and double vision. The left eyelid is drooped, the eye rests down and outward, and the left pupil is larger and reacts sluggishly to light. She has diabetes, but her previous eye examinations were normal. Strength and speech are intact. What is the most appropriate next action?

options.text: Schedule nonurgent orbital imaging six weeks later
options.explanation: An orbital study might address selected causes of ocular dysfunction, but delayed local imaging does not adequately evaluate the urgent possibility of an intracranial compressive aneurysm.

options.text: Arrange urgent intracranial vascular imaging and specialist evaluation
options.explanation: A new painful pupil-involving third nerve palsy raises concern for an aneurysmal compressive lesion and requires urgent evaluation despite coexisting diabetes.

options.text: Attribute the deficit to diabetes and reassess in three months
options.explanation: Diabetes increases microvascular palsy risk but does not safely explain away an acute painful pupil-involving pattern that may signal a compressive aneurysm.

options.text: Treat dry eye alone and continue normal activity
options.explanation: Ocular surface irritation does not produce third-nerve muscle weakness with ptosis and a dilated poorly reactive pupil in this neurological pattern.

explanation: The third nerve controls eyelid elevation, most extraocular movements, and parasympathetic pupillary constriction. Compression, particularly from an adjacent aneurysm, can affect the superficial pupillary fibers and produce a painful dilated-pupil palsy. Diabetes does not remove the need for urgent imaging in this presentation. Although pupil findings alone cannot perfectly distinguish all etiologies, the clinical combination warrants emergency vascular assessment. The intact limb examination is reassuring only about those functions; it does not exclude a local intracranial lesion with risk of rupture.
objective: Urgently investigate a new painful pupil-involving third nerve palsy for an intracranial compressive vascular lesion.
keyPoints: A focal cranial neuropathy can be a vascular emergency.
Diabetes is a risk factor, not a reason to bypass evaluation.

subject: Neurology
stem: A 33-year-old man is diagnosed with an acute isolated peripheral facial nerve palsy after appropriate examination. He cannot wrinkle his right forehead or fully close the right eye. There is no limb weakness, vesicular rash, hearing loss, or corneal injury yet. Etiology-directed medication has been discussed. Which additional measure is important immediately to prevent a foreseeable complication?

options.text: Institute eye lubrication and a safe eyelid-protection plan
options.explanation: Incomplete closure exposes the cornea to drying and injury, so lubrication and appropriate protection are needed while facial motor function recovers.

options.text: Wait for corneal pain before offering any eye care
options.explanation: Exposure injury can develop before severe symptoms prompt return, and prevention is appropriate once impaired eyelid closure is established on examination.

options.text: Use topical anesthetic eye drops repeatedly at home
options.explanation: Repeated anesthetic use can harm the cornea and mask injury; it does not provide the protective lubrication and closure support needed.

options.text: Prescribe only facial strengthening exercises without ocular precautions
options.explanation: Exercises do not immediately restore reliable eyelid closure, so relying on them alone leaves the exposed cornea vulnerable during the recovery period.

explanation: The facial nerve supplies the orbicularis oculi, and weakness can prevent complete eyelid closure. The resulting exposure risks corneal drying, abrasion, and more serious injury. Lubricating drops, appropriate nighttime ointment or closure protection, education, and reassessment are practical preventive measures, with eye specialist input when indicated. The exact plan should avoid pressure or taping techniques that injure the eye. This question does not assume every facial palsy is idiopathic; red flags and the cause still require assessment independently of immediate corneal protection.

stem: A 63-year-old woman presents with severe right ear pain followed by weakness of the entire right side of her face. She also notices reduced hearing and spinning dizziness. options.explanation: Although both cause peripheral facial weakness, the painful vesicular eruption and auditory or vestibular features point toward a specific infectious cause rather than idiopathic palsy.

options.explanation: Opioids are not preferred targeted abortive therapy for cluster headache and carry harms without reliably matching the short, rapidly escalating attack pattern.

stem: A 27-year-old woman has daily headaches, pulse-synchronous tinnitus, and seconds-long visual dimming when bending forward. Examination shows bilateral optic disc swelling but normal strength and alertness. Visual acuity is preserved between episodes. She recently began a tetracycline antibiotic for acne. options.explanation: Papilledema can threaten vision before profound loss develops, so deferring investigation until blindness would miss an opportunity to prevent permanent injury.

subject: Medicine
stem: A 75-year-old woman develops a new temporal headache, scalp tenderness, and jaw fatigue when chewing. Earlier today the vision in her right eye dimmed for several minutes. ESR and C-reactive protein are elevated. There is no fever or meningismus. A temporal artery biopsy can be arranged in four days. What is the most appropriate action now?

options.text: Begin urgent glucocorticoid treatment and arrange specialist confirmation
options.explanation: The clinical picture includes threatened ocular ischemia, so treatment should begin urgently while diagnostic confirmation and ophthalmic assessment are coordinated.

options.text: Withhold all treatment until the biopsy report is available
options.explanation: Waiting several days in a patient with transient visual loss risks irreversible ischemic injury and is not justified solely to preserve diagnostic testing.

options.text: Treat with a triptan and assume a first migraine at this age
options.explanation: New headache with jaw claudication and visual ischemic symptoms in an older adult requires evaluation for arteritis rather than uncritical migraine treatment.

options.text: Use antibiotics alone because inflammatory markers are elevated
options.explanation: Elevated inflammatory markers are nonspecific; the cranial ischemic pattern supports suspected arteritis, and antibiotics alone do not address this mechanism.

explanation: New headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, and transient visual loss in an older adult strongly suggest giant cell arteritis with threatened ocular ischemia. Glucocorticoids should be started urgently rather than waiting for biopsy, with immediate specialist input to determine the appropriate regimen and visual assessment. Biopsy or imaging remains important for confirmation and subsequent management. The case does not make inflammatory markers alone diagnostic; the clinical ischemic features drive urgency. stem: A 41-year-old woman taking topiramate for migraine prevention develops flank pain and passes a calcium phosphate stone. subject: Genetics
stem: A 34-year-old man has progressive chorea and executive dysfunction. His father developed genetically confirmed Huntington disease in his fifties. He has not taken dopamine-blocking drugs. options.explanation: An increase in the pathogenic CAG repeat can contribute to anticipation, in which disease manifests earlier in a subsequent generation despite autosomal dominant inheritance.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with stable multiple sclerosis notices blurred vision in a previously affected eye after spending twenty minutes in a hot bath. subject: Neurology
stem: A 23-year-old student has irresistible daytime sleep episodes despite a regular adequate sleep opportunity. When she laughs intensely, her knees buckle and her jaw briefly sags, but she remains aware of conversations and recalls the events. There is no postevent confusion. She sometimes experiences vivid dreamlike images while falling asleep. Which syndrome best fits the combination and warrants specialist sleep evaluation?

options.explanation: Emotion-triggered brief loss of tone with preserved awareness, combined with excessive daytime sleepiness and sleep-transition phenomena, suggests a narcolepsy syndrome with cataplexy.

explanation: Cataplexy is a sudden transient reduction of voluntary muscle tone, often triggered by strong emotion, with preserved consciousness. In the setting of excessive daytime sleepiness, it raises concern for narcolepsy type1. Sleep paralysis and vivid sleep-transition experiences may accompany the syndrome but are not independently diagnostic. Evaluation should confirm adequate sleep opportunity, review medications and other sleep disorders, and use appropriately prepared specialist testing. The vignette distinguishes muscle weakness from loss of consciousness; labeling every collapse as a seizure would obscure that decisive history and lead to an inappropriate workup.
objective: Recognize cataplexy from emotion-triggered brief atonia with preserved awareness in a patient with excessive daytime sleepiness.
keyPoints: Ask whether awareness is lost during a collapse.
Sleep-transition symptoms support but do not independently establish narcolepsy.

subject: Neurology
stem: Two days after a diagnostic lumbar puncture, a 34-year-old woman develops a headache that becomes severe within minutes of standing and improves substantially when she lies flat. She has mild neck discomfort but no fever, seizure, confusion, or focal deficit. The puncture site is clean, and no anticoagulants were used. Which diagnosis best explains this new procedure-associated positional headache?

options.text: Bacterial meningitis established solely by neck discomfort
options.explanation: Meningitis remains a concern with compatible features, but isolated mild neck discomfort with a strongly positional afebrile postprocedural pattern does not establish that diagnosis.

options.text: Medication-overuse headache after one dose of acetaminophen
options.explanation: A single analgesic exposure does not meet the sustained-use pattern associated with medication-overuse headache and cannot explain the immediate positional relationship.

options.text: A chronic cluster headache cycle
options.explanation: Cluster attacks have a different autonomic and temporal pattern and are not characteristically created by standing after lumbar puncture with relief on lying flat.

options.text: Post-dural puncture headache from cerebrospinal fluid leakage
options.explanation: The close timing after dural puncture and reproducible upright worsening with recumbent relief support a pressure-related headache caused by persistent cerebrospinal fluid leakage.

explanation: A dural puncture can permit continued cerebrospinal fluid leakage, producing a headache that is worse upright and relieved by lying down. The procedure history and positional pattern are stronger discriminators than the nonspecific neck discomfort. Persistent or disabling symptoms may warrant anesthesia review and consideration of an epidural blood patch after appropriate assessment. Fever, a changed nonpositional headache, neurological deficits, seizures, or altered consciousness require reevaluation for other complications. The diagnosis is not established by timing alone; it is supported by the full compatible clinical course.
objective: Recognize post-dural puncture headache from a new reproducible orthostatic pattern after lumbar puncture.
keyPoints: Procedure timing and posture are useful headache clues.
New red flags require reassessment rather than automatic attribution to a leak.

subject: Pharmacology
stem: A 74-year-old man receives cefepime for pneumonia. By day four his fever and oxygen requirement have improved, but creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 3.1 mg/dL. The original dose has not been adjusted. He develops confusion and multifocal myoclonus. Glucose and sodium are normal, and CT shows no acute lesion. Which diagnosis should be strongly considered during urgent medication review?

options.text: A new inherited Huntington disorder
options.explanation: An inherited progressive choreiform syndrome does not explain abrupt hospital-onset encephalopathy and myoclonus after a renally cleared medication accumulates.

options.text: An acute migraine aura without headache
options.explanation: The diffuse encephalopathy, multifocal myoclonus, renal deterioration, and drug exposure do not match a typical fully reversible sequential migraine aura pattern.

options.text: Cefepime-associated neurotoxicity during reduced renal clearance
options.explanation: Encephalopathy, myoclonus, and seizures are recognized cefepime toxicities, with renal impairment and unadjusted exposure increasing concern in this evolving clinical context.

options.text: Pneumonia progression proven by any new confusion
options.explanation: Infection can cause delirium, but improving respiratory findings and a new clearance problem make medication toxicity important rather than assuming infection progression.

explanation: Cefepime is renally cleared, and acute deterioration in kidney function can increase exposure if dosing is not reassessed. Its neurotoxicity can include altered consciousness, myoclonus, and seizures, including nonconvulsive status. Urgent medication adjustment or replacement, neurological assessment, and EEG when indicated are appropriate components of the response while other causes are evaluated. Toxicity can occasionally occur despite apparently adjusted doses, so a normal prescribing record does not universally exclude it. This case tests the importance of dynamic renal dosing rather than treating the admission creatinine as permanently valid.
objective: Consider cefepime neurotoxicity when new encephalopathy and myoclonus accompany renal decline during treatment.
keyPoints: Reassess renal dosing as function changes.
Improving infection does not exclude a new drug-related neurological problem.

subject: Psychiatry
stem: A 15-year-old boy has lost weight over four months after choking on a piece of meat. He now accepts only a few soft foods and avoids eating with friends. A swallowing evaluation finds no structural or physiological impairment. He wants to regain weight and denies fear of fatness or dissatisfaction with his body. Which diagnosis best explains the persistent restriction and nutritional impairment?

options.text: A normal transient food preference requiring no assessment
options.explanation: Four months of weight loss and social interference go beyond a harmless preference and require nutritional, medical, and psychological evaluation and support.

options.text: Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder
options.explanation: Restriction driven by fear of an aversive eating consequence, with nutritional and social impairment but no weight-shape drive, supports an avoidant/restrictive intake disorder.

options.text: Anorexia nervosa
options.explanation: Anorexia typically involves fear of weight gain or behavior preventing it and disturbed weight-related self-evaluation; this patient wants to regain weight and describes choking fear.

options.text: Bulimia nervosa
options.explanation: Bulimia involves recurrent binge eating and compensatory behaviors; neither is reported, and restriction here is linked to fear of choking rather than binges.

explanation: ARFID can arise from fear of choking or vomiting, sensory aversion, or low interest in eating. The restriction must lead to meaningful consequences such as nutritional deficiency, weight or growth impairment, reliance on supplements, or psychosocial disruption. Unlike anorexia nervosa, weight-shape preoccupation is not the driving feature. A negative swallowing evaluation supports considering a behavioral cause but does not eliminate the need to monitor medical stability and investigate new symptoms. Treatment planning should address both nutritional restoration and the maintaining fear, with developmentally appropriate family involvement.
objective: Recognize ARFID when fear of choking drives persistent nutritionally harmful restriction without weight-shape preoccupation.
keyPoints: Assess the motivation for restrictive eating.
Normal swallowing does not make nutritional impairment trivial.
